questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Colloid against true solution
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a colloid from a true solution
questions.stem: A dispersion scatters light, never settles, and passes through an ordinary filter paper. What places it in the colloid class rather than the true solution class?

options.text: its particles are larger than molecules yet small enough to stay dispersed and pass a filter
its particles carry charge, which is a property no true solution can have
options.misconception: believes charge is unique to colloids and impossible in solution

options.text: it scatters light, which no true solution does at any concentration
options.misconception: denies that a concentrated true solution can scatter light

options.text: its particles eventually settle, so it is really a suspension in waiting
options.misconception: confuses a colloid with a suspension that has not yet settled

questions.explanation: The classes are separated by particle size, not by appearance. Molecules and ions in a true solution are around a nanometre or less and never scatter a beam appreciably, while a suspension has particles large enough to settle and to be trapped by filter paper. Colloidal particles sit between those limits, roughly a nanometre to about a micrometre, large enough to scatter light and too small to sediment under gravity, which is why a colloid can look clear and still show a Tyndall beam. Charged particles are common in colloids but many true solutions are ionic too, so charge is not the test.
questions.hint: Ask what size the dispersed particles have relative to a filter pore and to a molecule.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: What the Tyndall effect evidences
questions.learningObjective: interpret the visible cone of a light beam in a dispersion
questions.stem: A beam of light is passed through a dispersion and the path of the beam is visible as a bright cone. What does that observation show?

options.text: the dispersed particles are large enough to scatter the beam, which is the Tyndall effect
the dispersion absorbs the beam, so the cone is light that got through
options.misconception: reads the visible cone as transmission rather than scattering

options.text: the dispersion is a true solution whose molecules happen to be large
options.misconception: assumes a true solution can scatter a beam

options.text: the beam has reflected off the inner wall of the container
options.misconception: attributes the cone to reflection from the vessel

questions.explanation: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam by particles, and the visible cone is simply the scattered light reaching the eye from along the path of the beam. It is the standard classroom test that separates a colloid from a true solution, in which the beam is invisible because the molecules are too small to scatter it appreciably. It is also a rough size measurement, since strongly scattering suspensions show a bright cone and weakly scattering colloids a faint one. Absence of a cone is informative, presence of one is diagnostic, which is why the beam is switched on in a dark room for the test.
questions.hint: Ask why the beam is visible where it passes rather than only where it lands.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Micelle structure in a surfactant
questions.learningObjective: describe how a surfactant arranges in a micelle
questions.stem: Above its critical micelle concentration a surfactant in water assembles into micelles. How are the surfactant molecules arranged inside one?

options.text: hydrophobic tails gathered inward with the hydrophilic heads pointing out into the water
hydrophilic heads gathered inward with the hydrophobic tails pointing out
options.misconception: reverses the amphiphilic arrangement and puts the water-loving part inside

options.text: molecules spread evenly through the water as a single molecular layer
options.misconception: confuses a micelle with a surface film or an ordinary solution

options.text: molecules in a flat stack with every tail facing the surrounding water
options.misconception: imposes a rigid layered structure instead of a closed aggregate

questions.explanation: A surfactant is amphiphilic, with a water-loving head and a water-repelling tail, and in water the cheapest arrangement for the tails is to huddle together away from the solvent while the heads keep contact with it. That gives a roughly spherical particle with a hydrophobic core and a hydrophilic shell, which is where non-polar substances such as oils and greases can dissolve. Below the critical micelle concentration the molecules sit mainly at the air water interface as a monolayer, and the micelles appear only once that surface is saturated.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the molecule wants to avoid the water.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Sol against gel
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a sol from a gel among colloidal systems
questions.stem: A colloidal system in which solid particles stay dispersed in a liquid is a sol, while one in which a solid network immobilises liquid is a gel. What separates the two?

options.text: a gel has particles joined into a continuous network that will not flow, a sol keeps them free to move
a gel is always a true solution and a sol is always a coarse suspension
options.misconception: assigns true solution and suspension to the two colloidal types

options.text: a gel forms only from a solid and a sol forms only from a liquid
options.misconception: believes the state of the starting material alone decides the colloid type

options.text: a gel is transparent and a sol is opaque, so appearance is the deciding test
options.misconception: treats optical clarity as the definition of a colloid type

questions.explanation: Both are colloidal, and the difference is the connectivity of the dispersed phase. In a sol the particles are separate from one another and the system flows, so it behaves like a very fine suspension that never settles. In a gel the particles have grown into a continuous network that spans the container and immobilises the liquid inside it, so the system holds its shape and does not flow, which is why jelly and gelatin are the familiar examples. Turning a sol into a gel is what happens when electrolytes are added to some colloids, since the charge that kept the particles apart is neutralised and they can link up.
questions.hint: Ask whether the dispersed particles touch one another or remain independent.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Cause of Brownian motion
questions.learningObjective: explain the random motion of colloidal particles
questions.stem: Particles in a colloid jostle about irregularly and never come to rest. What causes that movement?

options.text: molecules of the medium strike the particles unevenly from all sides at every instant
the particles are heavier than the medium, so they sink slowly at a steady rate
options.misconception: reads a random motion as slow steady settling

options.text: a stirring rod left running slowly in the vessel keeps them in motion
options.misconception: attributes the motion to an external mechanical source

options.text: the particles repel one another, so each moves away as fast as it approaches
options.misconception: explains a random walk as steady mutual repulsion

questions.explanation: Brownian motion is the jittering of a large particle suspended in a fluid, and it comes from the thermal motion of the many small molecules around it. At any instant the collisions are not perfectly balanced, so there is a net impulse, and the next instant the pattern is different, which makes the path erratic rather than directed. This is the direct experimental evidence for the random motion of molecules, since the jiggling is far too fast and irregular to be anything else. It does not overcome gravity, which is why a colloid diffuses and jitters but does not settle.
questions.hint: Ask what is hitting the particle many millions of times a second.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a colloid stays dispersed
questions.learningObjective: explain the stability of a charged colloidal dispersion
questions.stem: A colloidal dispersion stays dispersed for months because its particles carry charges of the same sign. What is that charge doing?

options.text: it holds the particles apart by repulsion, so they never grow into settling aggregates
it draws neighbouring particles together so that they clump into one large phase
options.misconception: believes like charge promotes aggregation of colloid particles

options.text: it dissolves the particles fully, converting the colloid into a true solution
options.misconception: claims colloidal charge turns a colloid into a true solution

options.text: it neutralises the surface charge and so removes the barrier to coagulation
options.misconception: confuses the charge that stabilises a colloid with the one that destroys it

questions.explanation: Most colloidal particles adsorb ions from the medium, and the counterions in the diffuse layer are only loosely bound, so the surface of every particle carries a net charge of the same sign. Two such particles brought close repel, and since the repulsive range is comparable to the particle size, they cannot approach closely enough for van der Waals attraction to capture them. Add electrolyte and the screening compresses that range until attraction wins, and the dispersion coagulates, which is the basis of the kitchen test in which salt breaks an emulsified dressing.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when two particles carrying the same sign are brought together.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Phase and phase boundary
questions.learningObjective: define a phase boundary and distinguish physical from chemical change
questions.stem: Ice and liquid water coexist in a closed flask at 0 degrees Celsius. What does the surface between the two regions represent?

options.text: a phase transition between two phases of one substance, with the two forms meeting at an interface
a chemical reaction in which the bonding of the water is being converted
options.misconception: reads a physical change as a chemical reaction

options.text: a boundary between two different substances that must always react on contact
options.misconception: insists any interface must separate different substances

options.text: the point at which the liquid has been used up and only solid remains
options.misconception: misreads a point of coexistence as a point of completion

questions.explanation: A phase is a region of a system with uniform physical properties, and the boundary between two phases of the same substance is where those properties change without the chemical identity changing. Ice and water are both the same molecule, so no bonds are made or broken, which is what makes it a physical change and what allows the two to coexist indefinitely at the melting point. Contrast a gas and its liquid, where two different substances are present and the interface is a site of chemical exchange, or at least of indefinite mixing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the chemical identity of the substance changes across the boundary.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Miscible against immiscible liquids
questions.learningObjective: distinguish miscible from immiscible liquid pairs
questions.stem: Two liquids that will not form a single homogeneous phase at any ratio are described as which of the following?

options.text: immiscible, separating into layers because attraction between like molecules prevails
miscible, dissolving in one another at every ratio the components permit
options.misconception: reverses the two terms so immiscibility is called miscibility

options.text: colloidal, staying dispersed as particles rather than forming two layers
options.misconception: confuses immiscibility with a colloidal dispersion

options.text: miscible only when hot, which is what immiscibility always turns out to mean
options.misconception: assumes every immiscible pair becomes miscible on heating

questions.explanation: Miscibility is decided by whether the attractions between two molecules of the same liquid outweigh those between unlike molecules, since mixing is favoured when the unlike attractions are comparable or stronger. Water and hexane, for example, have a hydrogen bonded network on one side and only dispersion forces on the other, so the unlike attraction is too weak to pay the cost of breaking the water network, and two layers form. Adding a third component such as a surfactant bridges the two and lets the pair form an emulsion, which is a dispersed system and not true miscibility.
questions.hint: Compare the attractions available within each liquid with those between them.

questions.topic: Theoretical yield from the limiting reagent
questions.learningObjective: find the theoretical product amount from a limiting reactant
questions.stem: An equation needs 1 mol of reactant A for every 2 mol of reactant B to give 1 mol of product. A 2.00 mol portion of A is mixed with 5.00 mol of B. What is the theoretical yield of product, in moles? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A supports 2.00 mol divided by its coefficient of 1, that is 2.00 mol of reaction, while B supports 5.00 mol divided by its coefficient of 2, that is 2.50 mol of reaction, so A is limiting and, with a product coefficient of 1, the yield is 2.00 mol. Working it as consumption instead, the 2.00 mol of A would need 4.00 mol of B and 1.00 mol of B is left over, confirming the same answer. The error to watch is dividing by a coefficient of 2 that belongs to the other reactant, which would make the more plentiful reagent look limiting.
questions.hint: For each reactant, divide its moles by its own coefficient, then take the smaller.

questions.topic: Efficiency of a photovoltaic panel

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a catalyst leaves the equilibrium alone
questions.learningObjective: explain why a catalyst does not move the equilibrium position
questions.stem: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction. Why does that leave the position of the equilibrium untouched?

options.text: it lowers the forward and reverse barriers alike, so both directions speed up and the constant is unchanged
it lowers only the forward barrier, which shifts the equilibrium towards the products
options.misconception: thinks a one-sided barrier change moves the equilibrium

options.text: it raises the equilibrium constant because more product is formed in a given time
options.misconception: assumes a faster reaction implies a larger equilibrium constant

options.text: it removes the barrier so far that the reaction becomes effectively complete
options.misconception: confuses a fast reaction with a complete one

questions.explanation: A catalyst works by offering an alternative route with lower barriers, and it lowers the barrier for the forward and the reverse reactions together, because the same alternative route can be run in either direction. Equilibrium depends on the difference between the two barriers, through the exponential of that difference divided by the thermal energy, and lowering both leaves the difference unchanged. That is why a catalyst changes how fast equilibrium is reached and never where it settles, and why a plant gains throughput rather than yield from adding one.
questions.hint: A catalyst offers an alternative route, and that route works in both directions.

questions.topic: Why a catalyst does not raise the yield
questions.learningObjective: explain why a catalyst changes rate but not equilibrium yield
questions.stem: Explain why adding a catalyst to an industrial reactor raises its throughput while leaving the equilibrium yield of the reaction unchanged.

answer.exemplar: A catalyst works by opening an alternative reaction route whose activation barriers are lower than those of the uncatalysed route, and the barriers of the forward and reverse steps fall by the same amount, because the alternative surface can carry either direction. What changes is how quickly the system gets to equilibrium, so a plant with a catalyst holds a larger amount of material mid-reaction at any moment and can run a smaller reactor or a faster cycle for the same output. A second, non-thermodynamic benefit is that the mild conditions a catalyst permits reduce side reactions, so selectivity can genuinely improve, and selectivity improvements do raise the yield of a chosen product. The distinction to keep is between the equilibrium position, which no catalyst moves, and the route, which it changes completely.

questions.topic: Mass percent after diluting a solution
questions.learningObjective: recompute a mass percent after adding solvent
questions.stem: A 20.0 g sample of a solution that is 5.00 percent solute by mass is made up to 100.0 mL with water of density 1.00 g/mL. What mass percent does the resulting solution have?

5.00 percent
options.misconception: ignores the dilution and reports the original percent

options.misconception: divides the solute mass by the solvent mass alone as the base

options.text: 4.00 percent
options.misconception: subtracts the solute percent from the original percent

questions.explanation: The 20.0 g portion contains 5.00 percent of 20.0 g, that is 1.00 g of solute, and adding water to reach 100.0 mL at 1.00 g/mL leaves 100.0 g of solution, so the percent is 1.00 g over 100.0 g, that is 1.00 percent. questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why recrystallisation needs a temperature-dependent solubility
questions.learningObjective: explain the requirement for a solubility that changes with temperature
questions.stem: Recrystallisation works only because the solubility of the solute changes with temperature. What would follow if a solute dissolved equally well in hot and in cold solvent?

options.text: the hot solution would stay saturated on cooling and no crystals would form to separate
crystals would form faster but be smaller and less pure than usual
options.misconception: blames rate and crystal size rather than the solubility change

options.text: more crystals would form, since cooling always increases the recovery
options.misconception: assumes cooling raises solubility for every solute

options.text: the solvent would evaporate faster and leave a purer solid behind
options.misconception: explains the separation by evaporation rather than solubility

questions.explanation: The separation comes entirely from the gap between the solubility at the boiling point of the solvent and the solubility at room temperature. Dissolve in the minimum of hot solvent to get close to saturation, cool, and the wanted compound comes out of solution while the impurity stays in. If the solubility barely changed, the cooling would precipitate nothing or everything, and in the first case there is no solid to collect at all. That is why a solvent is screened before use and why an ideal solvent is hot-soluble, cold-insoluble, and does not react with the compound.
questions.hint: Ask what the cooling step is supposed to push out of solution.

questions.topic: What limits the purity of a distillate
questions.learningObjective: explain why a simple distillation gives an impure first fraction
questions.stem: A simple distillation separates two miscible liquids that differ in boiling point. What limits the purity of the liquid collected?

options.text: a vapour rich in the lower boiler distils over first but it is never quite pure
the two liquids need the same boiling point for distillation to separate them
options.misconception: reverses the requirement, thinking equal boiling points help

options.text: the higher boiler must be trapped while the vapour is condensed as vapour
options.misconception: confuses the vapour and liquid phases during collection

options.text: the distillate is pure only if the higher boiler is heated harder than the lower
options.misconception: thinks stronger heating of the less volatile liquid purifies the distillate

questions.explanation: The vapour that leaves a pot boiling mixture is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid is, but it is not pure, so the first liquid to distil over carries some of the less volatile component with it. As the pot empties the composition of the vapour changes, and the last material out is rich in the higher boiler. A fractionating column exploits the repeated condensing and re-vapourising of that vapour to give successive plates of enrichment, and a simple distillation without a column is limited to separations where the boiling points are far apart.
questions.hint: Ask whether the vapour leaving a mixture is ever a pure component.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Operating window for an industrial catalyst
questions.learningObjective: state why an industrial catalyst has an economic temperature window
questions.stem: An industrial catalyst is only useful over a temperature range that is neither too low nor too high. Why does such a window exist?

options.text: rate sets the lower limit and catalyst survival, yield and cost set the upper one
the best temperature is the highest the catalyst survives, since rate rises with heat
options.misconception: ignores yield and lifetime in favour of rate alone

options.text: the best temperature is the lowest usable, since cool conditions always protect it
options.misconception: assumes a low temperature is always better

options.text: no window exists, since a catalyst works equally well at every temperature
options.misconception: believes catalysts are insensitive to temperature

questions.explanation: At low temperature the reaction is too slow to be economic, and at high temperature the catalyst can sinter, volatilise, coke or lose selectivity, while the equilibrium position itself may move against the wanted product. The operating point is therefore a compromise chosen with the reaction kinetics, the deactivation rate and the cost of heating all in view, and an industrial catalyst is engineered to widen that window rather than to maximise activity at a single temperature. A catalyst that is superb at one temperature and dies at the next slightly higher one is commercially useless.
questions.hint: Ask what stops the plant from simply running hotter and hotter.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Choosing the efficiency expression
questions.learningObjective: select the expression that defines a conversion efficiency
questions.stem: A photovoltaic cell delivers electrical power while receiving incident optical power. Which expression gives its efficiency?

options.text: the electrical power delivered divided by the optical power received
the optical power received divided by the electrical power delivered
options.misconception: inverts the ratio so a poor cell scores above one hundred percent

options.text: the electrical power delivered divided by the illuminated area
options.misconception: divides by area and produces a flux rather than a fraction

options.text: the optical power received divided by the illuminated area
options.misconception: reports the incident flux and never compares it with the output

questions.explanation: Efficiency is a ratio of what comes out to what goes in, so the useful output sits in the numerator and the input in the denominator, and the quotient is a pure number between zero and one. Inverting the ratio, as the second option does, produces a figure above one for any cell that loses power, which is a quick way to recognise the error. The area appears in how the incident power is obtained, from the irradiance times the area, but once that power in watts is known the area itself no longer belongs in the efficiency.
questions.hint: A ratio of useful output to input cannot exceed one, which tells you the order.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Expression for the product amount from a limiting reagent
questions.learningObjective: select the expression that gives the maximum product amount
questions.stem: Given the available moles of two reactants and the balanced equation, which expression gives the maximum moles of product?

options.text: divide each available amount by its coefficient, take the smaller, and multiply by the product coefficient
divide each available amount by its coefficient and take the larger result
options.misconception: picks the reactant in greatest excess as the limiting one

options.text: multiply each available amount by its coefficient and take the smaller
options.misconception: multiplies by the coefficient where it should divide

options.text: take the reactant of smaller available mass without using the equation
options.misconception: ignores stoichiometry and compares masses directly

questions.explanation: Each reactant supports a certain number of moles of reaction once its coefficient is taken into account, and the reaction can only go as far as the smaller of those supports, so the smallest quotient names the limiting reagent. The product amount then follows from that extent times its own coefficient, which is the step most often left out, giving an answer a factor of the product coefficient too small. Multiplying by the coefficients instead of dividing reverses the comparison entirely and reliably selects the wrong reagent.
questions.hint: The smallest quotient of available moles over coefficient identifies the reagent that runs out.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Melting point above the accepted value
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a melting point reported above the literature value
questions.stem: A purified solid is reported with a melting point higher than the accepted value for that compound. What does the claim suggest?

options.text: the sample may still carry solid impurity, or the transition was read too late
the sample must contain dissolved solvent, since any dissolved material raises the melting point
options.misconception: believes dissolved material always raises a melting point

options.text: the thermometer must be replaced, since no compound can melt above its literature value
options.misconception: treats the literature value as a hard instrument limit

options.text: the value is acceptable and shows the product is purer than the reference sample
options.misconception: reads an out-of-range melting point as extra purity

questions.explanation: A pure crystalline compound melts sharply at its accepted value, and the presence of a second solid raises and broadens the melting range because the melt is depressed by the dissolved impurity. A figure above the accepted value is therefore not a purity certificate; it usually means the sample is not what it is claimed to be, or that the transition was taken to have started or ended at the wrong point because the heating was too fast or the thermometer was badly placed. A wide range is as diagnostic as a high number, and both together are worse news than either alone.
questions.hint: Ask what a pure crystalline sample must do, and what a second solid phase does to it.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a colloid neither settles nor scatters light away
questions.learningObjective: explain colloidal stability and the Tyndall observation together
questions.stem: Explain why a colloidal dispersion does not settle, and what the Tyndall effect tells you about the particles responsible for that behaviour.

answer.exemplar: Two things keep a colloid dispersed. The particles are large enough that gravity would eventually pull them down, but small enough, typically between about a nanometre and a micrometre, that the random thermal motion of the medium pushes them around as hard as gravity pulls them down, so the downward drift is imperceptible. They are also usually charged, with ions adsorbed from the medium, and the resulting mutual repulsion keeps any two particles from approaching closely enough for dispersion forces to capture them and grow them into a settling aggregate. The same size range explains the light. Particles that size are comparable with the wavelength of visible light and scatter it efficiently, so a beam becomes visible along its path, which is the Tyndall effect, whereas molecules in a true solution are far too small to scatter it appreciably and the beam stays invisible. Add electrolyte and the charges are screened, the repulsion range collapses, the particles aggregate, and the dispersion coagulates, which is the practical demonstration that the charge was doing the stabilising.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Fractions kept and discarded in a distillation
questions.learningObjective: explain why the first and last distillate fractions are discarded
questions.stem: Explain why a distiller collects the middle fractions from a distillation and discards what comes out at the very beginning and at the very end.

answer.exemplar: The liquid leaving a pot boiling a mixture is never a pure component. Early on it is enriched in the more volatile material but still carries a substantial fraction of the less volatile one, so the first fraction is a mixture and would contaminate anything collected into it. Waiting until the still head temperature has settled and a small test portion has been checked lets that mixture go, and the composition of what distils over then approaches that of the vapour in equilibrium with the pot, which is much closer to the wanted product. At the other end the pot has become rich in the higher boiler, the last material out is largely that impurity, and distilling it into the receiver would put the impurity straight back into the product. Discarding the tails therefore protects purity at the cost of some yield, which is the trade a plant makes whenever the specification is tight. The same argument explains why a fractionating column improves matters, since its plates enrich the vapour repeatedly before it ever reaches the condenser.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why doping raises the conductivity of a semiconductor
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of doping on semiconductor conductivity
questions.stem: Explain why adding a small amount of a suitable impurity to a semiconductor can increase its conductivity by many orders of magnitude.

answer.exemplar: In an intrinsic semiconductor the number of mobile carriers is set by how far the top of the valence band lies below the bottom of the conduction band, and at ordinary temperatures that thermal excitation produces very few of them, so the conductivity is small. Doping replaces some lattice atoms with atoms of a neighbouring group, which changes the electron count of the bonds rather than the bonding itself. A group 15 atom in a group 14 lattice has one valence electron too many and can contribute it to the conduction band without disturbing the four bonds, and a group 14 atom in the same lattice leaves a vacancy, or hole, in the valence band. Either way the concentration of mobile carriers is raised from roughly one in ten billion to something like one in a thousand, and because conductivity is proportional to the number of carriers and to their mobility, the increase is enormous. The dopant is deliberately dilute, since a heavily doped material stops behaving as a semiconductor and the point is to add carriers without disturbing the lattice.
